{{Short description|Shinto shrine in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sumiyoshi Shrine
住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sumiyoshi Shrine
住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sumiyoshi Shrine
住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sumiyoshi Shrine
住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sumiyoshi Shrine
住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sumiyoshi Shrine
住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sumiyoshi Shrine
住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sumiyoshi Shrine
住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) {{Short description|Shinto shrine in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sumiyoshi Shrine
住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) torii.JPG|Torii Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka), honden.JPG|Honden (ICP) Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) nougakuden.JPG|Noh Theatre ==See also== *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category|Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka)}} *[https://www.nihondaiichisumiyoshigu.jp Official home page]{{in lang|ja}} *[https://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/93 Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City]{{in lang|ja}} *[https://www.crossroadfukuoka.jp/spot/12552 Fukuoka Tourism Web]{{in lang|ja}} {{Shinto shrine}} ]] ]] {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Ichinomiya}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Shinto shrines in Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Chikuzen Province]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Fukuoka]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kanpei Shōsha]] [[Category:Shrines dedicated to empress Jingū]] [[Category:Sumiyoshi shrines]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 6]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:11 6]] [[Category:mm]] [[Category:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]] [[Category:bump 1-26]] [[Category:kk]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:C111]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] }} [[sn:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]] [[en:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]] [[ja:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]]

The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. 住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. 住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was Ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd Rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) torii.JPG|Torii Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka), honden.JPG|Honden (ICP) Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) nougakuden.JPG|Noh Theatre ==See also== *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category|Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka)}} *[https://www.nihondaiichisumiyoshigu.jp Official home page]{{in lang|ja}} *[https://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/93 Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City]{{in lang|ja}} *[https://www.crossroadfukuoka.jp/spot/12552 Fukuoka Tourism Web]{{in lang|ja}} {{Shinto shrine}} ]] {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Ichinomiya}} {{draft categories| }} {{draft categories| [[Category:Shinto shrines in Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Chikuzen Province]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Fukuoka]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kanpei Shōsha]] [[Category:Shrines dedicated to empress Jingū]] [[Category:Sumiyoshi shrines]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 6]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] }} [[sn:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]] [[en:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]] [[ja:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]]

It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was Ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd Rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark. The pillars are painted vermilion and the wooden walls are painted white. It was designated as a National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]] in 1922.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/3464|title=住吉神社本殿|language=ja |publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs |accessdate=December 20, 2023}} ==Gallery== Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) torii.JPG|Torii Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka), honden.JPG|Honden (ICP) Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) nougakuden.JPG|Noh Theatre ==See also== *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category|Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka)}} *[https://www.nihondaiichisumiyoshigu.jp Official home page]{{in lang|ja}} *[https://bunkazai.city.fukuoka.lg.jp/cultural_properties/detail/93 Cultural Properties of Fukuoka City]{{in lang|ja}} *[https://www.crossroadfukuoka.jp/spot/12552 Fukuoka Tourism Web]{{in lang|ja}} {{Shinto shrine}} ]] {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Ichinomiya}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Shinto shrines in Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:Chikuzen Province]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Fukuoka]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kanpei Shōsha]] [[Category:Shrines dedicated to empress Jingū]] [[Category:Sumiyoshi shrines]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 6]] [[Category:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] [[sn:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]]}} [[sn:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]] [[en:Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]] [[sn:umiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)]] [[sn: failed]]

{{Short description|Shinto shrine in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Sumiyoshi Shrine
住吉神社 | image = Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka) haiden-1.JPG | caption = Haiden of Sumiyoshi Shrine {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Fukuoka Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|35|9.26|N|130|24|49.33|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Sumiyoshi Shrine | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Sumiyoshi | deity = [[Sumiyoshi sanjin]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 3-1-51 Sumiyoshi, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka-shi, Fukuoka-ken | website = | architecture_style = Sumiyoshi-zukuri | festival = October 13 | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Sumiyoshi Shrine'''|住吉神社}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the Sumiyoshi neighborhood of [[Hakata-ku, Fukuoka]] in [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Chikuzen Province]]. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on October 13.{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Along with the more famous [[Sumiyoshi-taisha]] in [[Osaka]] and the [[Sumiyoshi Shrine (Shimonoseki)|Sumiyoshi Jinja]] in [[Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi]], it is one of the "Three Great Sumiyoshi" shrines.{{cite encyclopedia|last=Yonei|first=Teruyoshi|title=Aramitama|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1180|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=5 February 2011}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Sumiyoshi Jinja are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Sumiyoshi sanjin]]'''| 住吉三神|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Empress Jingū]]'''| 神功皇后|}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照皇大神 |}} ==Origins== Per the shrine's legend (''Chikuzen Sumiyoshi Daimyojin Goengi''), the shrine is the birthplace of the Sumiyoshi cult and the origin for all Sumiyoshi shrines in the country. Unlike Hakata, which is located on sand dunes, the area surrounding the shrine grounds is located on the alluvial land of the Naka River, and topographically located on the cape of Reizeitsu, which juts out into the mouths of the Hie River and the Naka River. This was thought to be a suitable location for a place of worship for the guardian deity of navigation. Bronze spear and a bronze sword from the [[Yayoi Period]] have been excavated from the shrine grounds, and it is theorized that this area was originally a sacred place for [[Nakoku]] or the Amabe maritime tribe. ==History== The foundation of the Sumitomo Shrine in Hakozaki is unknown. It first appears in historical documentation in an entry in the ''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' dated April 737, when it is recorded that offerings were made to "Chikushi Sumiyoshi" and to [[Ise Grand Shrine]] in response to disrespectful actions by the kingdom of [[Silla]] in the [[Korean Peninsula]]. Per a survey dated 806, 36 shrines were dedicated to Sumiyoshi in Chikuzen Province, and in 847 the monk [[Ennin]] and in 852 the monk [[Enchin]] recited Buddhist sutras at the shrine on their return from [[Tang China]]. In 878, it was placed under the direct protection of the Imperial Court after an oracle at [[ Kashii-gū]] warned of a possible attack by Silla. In the ''[[Engishiki]]'', the shrine is listed as a ''Myojin Taisha'' and in 1019, the shrine was entrusted to [[Emperor Go-Ichijō]] as a "once-in-a-generation" offering. It has been regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of Chikuzen Province since the late [[Heian period]]. [[Takezaki Suenaga]]'s ''[[Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba]]'' depicts the vermilion torii gate of Sumiyoshi Shrine. In 1480, the ''[[renga]]'' master [[Sōgi]] visited the shrine, and wrote about the devastation of Sumiyoshi Shrine due to war in the "Tsukushi Doki". During the [[Sengoku period]], the shrine records and old documents were taken by [[Ōuchi Yoshitaka]] to [[Yamaguchi, Yamaguchi|Yamaguchi]] and were destroyed in the [[Tainei-ji incident]] of 1551. The current shrine was restored by [[Kuroda Nagamasa]], the first ''[[daimyō]]'' of [[Fukuoka Domain]] in 1623. Subsequent rulers of the domain continued to support the shrine to the [[Meiji Restoration|Meiji restoration]]. Under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]]'s system of [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Ranked Shinto shrines]], Sumiyoshi Shrine was Ranked as a Prefectural Shrine in 1872, and promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 3rd Rank|官幣小社|Kanpei-shōsha}} in 1925. In 2004, [[archaeological excavation]]s began around the precincts. In a total of three excavations up to 2014, the remains of a mansion from the medieval to early modern period were discovered along with artifacts related to rituals. ==Cultural Properties== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿||}} - The main hall of the shrine was built by Kuroda Nagamasa in 1623 during the early Edo period. It is in the ''Sumiyoshi-zukuri'' style, which is considered to be an older form of shrine architecture. It is a gabled structure and the roof is thatched with cypress bark.
